THE SESSION'S EARLIER GUESSES AND HYPOTHESES:
  [Y1] guess: UDP fills the sender-side FIFO queue, so TCP SYN/data packets are tail-dropped before reaching the receiver; no SYN-ACK or data ACKs are produced, and the 3 retransmissions are TCP retries that never establish delivery.
  [Y2] guess: TcpCubic's loss/RTO response makes the TCP sender stop after a few retries; a different TCP congestion control could deliver data despite the same FIFO queue.
  [Y3] guess: The queue length 100 is too short to admit TCP packets before UDP fills it; a much longer FIFO queue would let TCP handshake and deliver some data.
  [Y4] guess: The scheduler queue gives UDP and TCP roughly equal service on l1, so TCP can establish and its goodput is capped near half the 1Gbps link rather than by the FIFO queue length.
  [Y5] guess: A 1000-packet FIFO still lets UDP monopolize the link; TCP only slips through during rare queue gaps and loses most ACKs, so it remains in RTO/probe state and delivers only a few bytes.
  [Y6] guess: Under the FIFO queue TCP never receives ACKs, so the congestion-control algorithm is not engaged beyond initial retries; BBR cannot change the outcome.
  [Y7] guess: Increasing the scheduler queue length to 1000 will reduce TCP queue drops/retransmissions and raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1%.
  [Y8] guess: Under a scheduler, TcpBbr's bandwidth probing will capture more than TcpCubic's fair share and raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1%.
  [Y9] guess: The scheduler caps each flow near its class share, so a longer queue mainly adds delay and slightly lowers Cubic's rate even though it removes TCP drops.
  [Y10] guess: BBR paces below its scheduler class share, leaving spare scheduler capacity to UDP; loss-based TCP that fills its class gets the fair share.
  [Y11] guess: Queue delay, not TCP drops, limits scheduler TCP; a 4-packet or 250-packet queue would reduce delay enough to raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1% over q100.
  [Y12] guess: TcpBic under scheduler can exceed TcpCubic by more than 1% by filling or probing the scheduler class better.
  [H1] hypothesis (supported): Replacing the sender-side FIFO queue with a scheduler queue will let TCP reach the receiver and deliver data, so tcp_goodput_bps becomes greater than 0.

THE SESSION'S EARLIER GUESSES AND HYPOTHESES:
  [Y1] guess: UDP fills the sender-side FIFO queue, so TCP SYN/data packets are tail-dropped before reaching the receiver; no SYN-ACK or data ACKs are produced, and the 3 retransmissions are TCP retries that never establish delivery.
  [Y2] guess: TcpCubic's loss/RTO response makes the TCP sender stop after a few retries; a different TCP congestion control could deliver data despite the same FIFO queue.
  [Y3] guess: The queue length 100 is too short to admit TCP packets before UDP fills it; a much longer FIFO queue would let TCP handshake and deliver some data.
  [Y4] guess: The scheduler queue gives UDP and TCP roughly equal service on l1, so TCP can establish and its goodput is capped near half the 1Gbps link rather than by the FIFO queue length.
  [Y5] guess: A 1000-packet FIFO still lets UDP monopolize the link; TCP only slips through during rare queue gaps and loses most ACKs, so it remains in RTO/probe state and delivers only a few bytes.
  [Y6] guess: Under the FIFO queue TCP never receives ACKs, so the congestion-control algorithm is not engaged beyond initial retries; BBR cannot change the outcome.
  [Y7] guess: Increasing the scheduler queue length to 1000 will reduce TCP queue drops/retransmissions and raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1%.
  [Y8] guess: Under a scheduler, TcpBbr's bandwidth probing will capture more than TcpCubic's fair share and raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1%.
  [Y9] guess: The scheduler caps each flow near its class share, so a longer queue mainly adds delay and slightly lowers Cubic's rate even though it removes TCP drops.
  [Y10] guess: BBR paces below its scheduler class share, leaving spare scheduler capacity to UDP; loss-based TCP that fills its class gets the fair share.
  [Y11] guess: Queue delay, not TCP drops, limits scheduler TCP; a 4-packet or 250-packet queue would reduce delay enough to raise tcp_goodput_bps by more than 1% over q100.

A guess may be wrong and still be sound here: you judge whether it starts from what was measured and adds something, not whether it is true. A guess that takes up an earlier one with a stated difference (another cause, another range, a reason why the earlier test was not fair) is not a repetition. This is not the researcher's first guess, and a later guess has to be the fruit of what was learned since the earlier ones. The records marked NEW are what it says it learned from. Say in your reasoning what they show that the earlier guesses did not have, and ask: would the researcher have made this same guess without them? If yes, the citation is for form only and the defect is not_from_what_was_learned.

Correct: say what the rule gives if the tested guess is true and the competing guess false, and what it gives if the competing guess is true and the tested guess false; pass only when the first is HELD and the second FAILED. THE SYSTEM, in the brief's words: A network of 2 hosts: sender, receiver. Link l1 joins sender and receiver: it carries 1Gbps with a one-way delay of 50us. On sender's side packets wait in one queue of the knob l1.queue.length packets; a packet that arrives when it is full is dropped. Flow udp is UDP from sender to receiver: packets of 1400 bytes at a constant rate (2 Gbps). Flow tcp is TCP from sender to receiver: it always has data to send; its congestion control is the knob tcp.type. A host with more than one link forwards packets. In each simulation the flows start within the first 10 ms, traffic runs for one second that is not measured, and then for duration seconds, over which the outputs are measured.

The simulations it compares differ only in what the claim is about, its measure can see it, and the competing guess explains the same result. Correct: say what the rule gives if the tested guess is true and the competing guess false, and what it gives if the competing guess is true and the tested guess false; pass only when the first is HELD and the second FAILED. Judge the competing guess the researcher named, do not replace it with your own. If the competing cause this test needs is a guess listed above other than the one the rule names, say so in feedback with its id; only if none of them states it, name it in missing. Last, feedback for the researcher: which question failed and the one problem that matters most, the record ids and numbers it rests on, and what a repaired test must achieve. The feedback never contains a decision rule, a measure@label, simulations or a network change: the researcher must find the repair itself. A test is not wanting for being small or for testing only one consequence of the guess.
